/-!
# Erdős Problem 412

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/412](https://www.erdosproblems.com/412)

Reviewed by @b-mehta on 2025-05-27
-/

open ArithmeticFunction.sigma

namespace Erdos412

/--
Let $σ_1(n)=σ(n)$, the sum of divisors function, and $σ_k(n) = σ(σ_{k-1}(n))$.
Is it true that, for every $m, n ≥ 2$, there exist some $i, j$ such that $σ_i(m) = σ_j(n)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_412 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᵉ (m ≥ 2) (n ≥ 2), ∃ i j, (σ 1)^[i] m = (σ 1)^[j] n := by
  sorry

end Erdos412

reformulations.difference: The existential indices are natural numbers and may be zero, so Lean allows the identity iterate rather than explicitly restricting to the positive iterates σ₁, σ₂, ….
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any self-map f, a meeting f^[i](m) = f^[j](n) gives f^[i+1](m) = f^[j+1](n) by applying f to both sides. Both new indices are positive. Conversely, positive-index witnesses are natural-index witnesses. Thus the pointwise conditions, and consequently the full universally quantified questions, are equivalent. Both equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/indices.lean without any sorryAx dependency.

review.notes:
The primary paper’s statement (vi), p. 169, asks whether every m,n > 1 have equal iterates, matching the Lean question. Checked the inferred natural-number domains, quantifier scope, answer placeholder, and function iteration (not arithmetic-function powers). Evaluations agree with the OEIS sequences. Lean checks establish σ(0)=0, σ(1)=1, and that all iterates starting at n ≥ 2 remain ≥ 2, so the default value at zero is unreachable.

Access limitation: the cited https://www.erdosproblems.com/412 page was blocked by Cloudflare despite descriptive User-Agent headers; the text-reader service was rate-limited. Its current remarks could not be read directly. Mathematical wording was verified against the primary paper instead, and the community database corroborates the recorded open status.
